Bo French’s Tweet and the Tempest in Texas
 
Plus, Trump says there’s no need for AI guardrails as long as he is in the White House, and why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline is roiling oil markets
 
 
CALLAGHAN O’HARE/REUTERS
 

Good morning. Bo French, a candidate for Texas’ railroad commissioner, is testing the boundaries of political speech in a moment when both parties are struggling to define what should be off limits.

 

On Saturday night, the University of Texas won a thrilling evening football game over the Ohio State University Buckeyes.

 

On Sunday, French posted a photograph of nonwhite UT fans cheering for their team. He wrote, “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

 

That’s when all hell broke loose.

 

Sen. John Cornyn, a Republican who lost his primary to Ken Paxton earlier this year, attacked French’s post and said, “This is the Republican nominee for statewide office. Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized? This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad.”

 

A number of other Texas Republicans joined Cornyn in condemning French. French later suggested that foreign-born students were flooding the flagship university. State law requires 90% of UT freshmen to be in-state, however.

 

In a radio interview Monday, French didn’t back down, saying, “It’s no surprise that the less-conservative people in Texas are the ones attacking me,” according to the Texas Tribune.

 

Paxton and his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, have waded into the matter and—predictably—used it to attack each other. Meanwhile, French is fundraising off it all and claims he’s now “inundated” with requests for yard signs.

 

Democrats have some experience with this. They have struggled for months to distance themselves from provocative streamer Hasan Piker, who at one point said the U.S. “deserved” 9/11 (Piker later tried to distance himself from those comments). Piker has campaigned with Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, and was at his primary night party.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Supreme Court: The high court blocked the Trump administration from imposing new requirements for mail ballots ahead of the midterm elections.

 

Mitch McConnell: The Kentucky senator returned to the Capitol after three months.

 

Donald Trump Jr.: A Russian businessman financed wedding celebrations of the president’s son.

 

Trump’s Tuesday: The president is scheduled to hold two policy meetings and participate in an ambassador credentialing ceremony in the Oval Office Tuesday afternoon.

What I’m Following

 
 
BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/GETTY IMAGES
 

AI doesn’t need guardrails while I’m president, Trump says. The president pushed back on the need for tighter federal regulations on artificial intelligence and dismissed safety concerns as a hoax that would leave the industry in financial ruin and hand China a competitive edge. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday. Industry leaders are sounding increasingly urgent warnings about the need for regulation to guard against potential dangers from their own technology.

 

What is Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline and why is it rocking oil markets? The kingdom is racing to repair a critical oil pipeline shut down by drone attacks last week. The disruption threatens to remove another major source of crude from global markets. The East-West pipeline has become one of the world’s most important pieces of energy infrastructure during the Iran war, a workaround to sharply curtailed tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Mamdani sues Trump administration over new immigration rule. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said a coalition of cities including New York filed a lawsuit challenging a new Trump administration rule regarding immigrants and public benefits. The rule—which takes effect Sept. 18—would let the federal government more easily deny green cards and visas to immigrants based on their use of public benefits.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The yield on the 10-year Treasury note hit 5% for just the second time since 2007.

 

• Kevin Warsh’s appointment ended Trump’s war with the Fed, but a rate hike would test the truce.

 

• The Environmental Protection Agency plans to repeal some carbon dioxide emission rules for power plants.

 

• Abbott Laboratories agreed to pay $385 million to settle allegations related to its management of a baby formula facility.

 

• U.S. sanctions Russia’s VTB Bank in latest target for campaign against Iran.
